ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the length of the line segment $AB$ is $a$. Extend the line segment $AB$ to $C$ so that $BC=b$. Let points $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. Find the length of $MN$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given that $AB=a$ and $BC=b$,\\
thus $AC=AB+BC=a+b$,\\
and since points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$ respectively,\\
thus $CM=\frac{1}{2}AC=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)$ and $CN=\frac{1}{2}BC=\frac{1}{2}b$,\\
thus $MN=CM-CN=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)-\frac{1}{2}b=\boxed{\frac{1}{2}a}$.

Since points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$ respectively, $CM=\frac{1}{2}AC=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)$ and $CN=\frac{1}{2}BC=\frac{1}{2}b$. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the attached figure there are three small diagrams, and diagram ③ on the right is the line segment schematic corresponding to this problem. Diagram ③ shows a horizontal straight line, with point A on the left, point C on the right, and point B located between A and C; point M and point N are also marked on the same straight line, among which N is located between B and C, and M is located between A and C. According to the problem statement, AB=a, line segment AB is extended to the right to C, and BC=b. Then reason: Because A, B, C are collinear and B is between A and C, AC=AB+BC=a+b. M is the midpoint of AC, so CM=AC/2=(a+b)/2. N is the midpoint of BC, so CN=BC/2=b/2. Looking leftward from C along the same straight line, the part by which the distance from M to C exceeds the distance from N to C is MN, therefore MN=CM-CN=(a+b)/2-b/2=a/2.
